entry.title: Autoresearch, Seven Months After My Grinder

link.title: Autoresearch, Seven Months After My Grinder

entry.content:
整理中 · Work in progress. These are working notes while I organize the original GrepQA experiments and refine the figures. The historical SOTA comparison has not been independently reproduced.

On April 1, I posted a skill called benchmark-grinder in a WeChat group. The pitch was simple: give Claude Code a benchmark, let it keep trying changes, and go to sleep. In the morning, read the git history. Seven months later, I came across Anthropic’s Automating eval design and hillclimbing with Claude, published on September 28. It packages a more carefully designed version of this workflow into /claude-api build-eval and /claude-api hillclimb.

I’m glad this exists. My skill was useful, but I hadn’t thought through the evaluation nearly as carefully. Reading Anthropic’s design sent me back to my own reports to see what I had actually built, and what the overnight runs had established.

The April version

The work started a little earlier than I remembered. My EPCC report is dated March 31, and the grinder repository’s first commit is from that evening. The slides mention NVIDIA’s AVO, AlphaEvolve, and Karpathy’s autoresearch. I was borrowing a workflow and making it reusable for my own experiments.

There were two loops. auto-research-single read papers and revised ideas, keeping its working memory in Markdown files. benchmark-grinder worked against an executable evaluation. It recorded the metric, run command, allowed edits, and frozen evaluation files in benchmark.md; ran an untouched baseline; tried one hypothesis at a time; and kept or discarded the change. Logs and a result ledger preserved what happened. I’ve put the relevant four slides here and archived the original skill text, so the sources don’t depend on access to my private repositories.

The skill already prohibited gaming the evaluator and warned against unsupported gains in noisy runs. It also allowed a simpler or cheaper system to count as progress at roughly equal quality. The unfinished part was turning those intentions into a measurement protocol: it had no prescribed data split, grader calibration, or statistical acceptance rule.

The first overnight log was modest: 29.76% F1 became 30.07%, and one attempt crashed with an SSL error. The more substantial example came next, when I used the same style of repeated experimentation on GrepQA: ask an LLM for keyword predicates, search the conversation text, then answer from the retrieved evidence.

GrepQA’s longer run

My memory was “about 32 versions.” The historical repository record actually reaches v33, and the source later includes v34, an answer-routing variant with latency analysis. The retained winner was v21. In the main results table, GrepQA went from 29.90 to 51.69 F1, a gain of 21.79 percentage points. The full-context configuration in that table scored 42.39. These were reported GPT-4o-mini runs on LoCoMo-10; the April 8 report slides preserve the architecture and results.

The improvements had identifiable mechanisms. Context windows brought neighboring turns into view. Multiple predicates and a must/should scoring scheme improved retrieval. Session dates helped resolve relative time in answers. The retained v21 used three predicates derived from the question and removed answer-side keyword guessing: guessing an answer before retrieval could send the search toward the wrong evidence.

This was the result I remembered as reaching SOTA. In the report’s comparison table, 51.69 was above the imported memory-system results, including Mem0 at 45.10 and its graph variant at 46.14. Those were literature numbers, and the historical README explicitly notes differences in model and evaluation setup. The defensible claim here is that GrepQA exceeded the published numbers in that comparison, and substantially improved my own recorded baseline; this is not a newly verified, controlled leaderboard result.

The plateau is part of the story too. Versions v22–v33 explored IDF scoring, date anchors, enumeration, reranking, and session selection without displacing v21 in the recorded full evaluation. Some trials were only pilots. The plot distinguishes those cases; a missing score means the artifact was not recovered, not that the method scored zero.

The complete version log

Here is the whole trail, including regressions and unfinished evidence. Full and pilot follow the source labels. Alt. marks conflicting or differently configured scores in the surviving records. The full-run table and changelog disagree for v6 and v13, so both numbers are retained rather than silently choosing one. “—” means I have not recovered a separate score. The source archive includes the changelogs, commit messages, and recovered module notes.

Version Recorded F1 Run What changed / what happened
v1 29.90 Full Baseline: single keyword predicate, top-k retrieval
v2 35.18 Full Sliding window context expansion + multi-query retrieval
v3 28.96 Full Precision-focused: window=0, top-k=2, reranking, smarter fallback
v4 22.43 Full Adaptive top-k + stricter answer extraction prompt
v5 31.51 Full Selective LLM filtering when many turns retrieved
v6 46.71 / 44.69 Alt. New engine: 2 predicates, must/should scoring, speaker filter. Main table / later log: 46.71. Original changelog: 44.69. Both retained here; configuration mapping is unresolved.
v7 41.62 Pilot Added session-date-aware time_hint scoring
v8 35.18 Pilot Answer-type-aware answering prompts
v9 44.57 Pilot Switched to 3 question-side predicates
v10 46.46 Full Date-aware answer prompt on top of v6-k8
v11 46.16 Full Answer prompt: include all values for list questions
v12 47.51 Full Balanced answer prompt: complete but concise
v13 48.10 / 51.34 Alt. Resolve relative time expressions using session timestamps. Changelog: 48.10. Historical selected full-run table: 51.34. The record does not reconcile these runs.
v14 47.46 Full Combined temporal reasoning with “be complete” instruction
v15 45.26 Pilot Answer-anticipation words added to predicate generation
v16 47.41 Pilot Conservative third answer-anticipation predicate
v17 44.06 Pilot Second predicate explicitly targets answer-turn vocabulary
v18 48.16 Full Disabled speaker fallback to reduce noisy retrieval
v19 46.48 Pilot Reduced top-k from 8 to 5 to cut retrieval noise
v20 45.69 Pilot 3 predicates including answer-side keyword guessing
v21 51.69 Full 3 predicates, question-side only; removed answer guessing. Retained winner: full 51.69; a later pilot baseline was 49.57. Pilot and full scores are different evaluations.
v22 — — Enforce single-word must_keywords, avoiding exact-match failures from multiword phrases. Source recovered; separate score not found.
v23 — — Retrieve top_k=20 and ask the answerer to enumerate all items. Not retained; separate score not found.
v24 — — Weight keyword matches by inverse document frequency (IDF). Not retained; separate score not found.
v25 — — If too few turns match, generate relaxed predicates for a second retrieval pass. Not retained; separate score not found.
v26 — — Use larger retrieval and enumerate-all answers only for list questions. Not retained; separate score not found.
v27 — — Add date anchors and vocabulary bridges to predicate generation. A later commit reports a pilot regression of about 5.4 pp; no absolute score recovered.
v28 — — Retrieve broadly, then have an LLM rerank down to the most relevant turns. Not retained; separate score not found.
v29 — — Inject a month/year predicate in Python while keeping the v21 prompt. Date matching initially searched turn text rather than session headers; separate score not found.
v30 — — Force shorter answers and lower the answer token limit from 64 to 48. Not retained; separate score not found.
v31 51.19 Pilot Include session dates in the text used to score predicates. Pilot 51.19 vs v21 pilot 49.57; later full run regressed 0.89 pp vs v21. Common words in headers introduced false matches.
v32 — — Score session headers only for predicates explicitly tagged as date anchors. Attempts to fix v31 interference; not retained. Separate score not found.
v33 46.99 Pilot Classify enumeration questions and generate diverse predicates for them. Pilot 46.99 vs v21 pilot 49.57 (−2.58 pp); not retained.
v34 — — Route temporal questions to concise answers and other questions to comprehensive answers. Implementation and latency analysis recovered; independent quality score not found.

One later attempt is particularly instructive. v31 looked promising on the pilot (51.19 against v21’s 49.57), then regressed on the full run. Scoring every turn together with its session header introduced unwanted keyword matches. v32 narrowed that behavior to date-anchor predicates. That is exactly the kind of history I want to retain: the attractive first signal, the broader failure, and the next hypothesis it suggested.

The process got me a useful system and a collection of failed explanations. Anthropic’s evaluation discipline would make the next such search easier to interpret, especially after many attempts on the same benchmark.

Anthropic’s design

The entry point matters. build-eval starts with representative cases, preferably grounded in production traffic or real failures, and asks the user to review inputs and sample grades. hillclimb then works within an agreed scope and objective, checks whether a useful gain is measurable above noise, and tests individual changes. The proposer uses training failures; held-out scores help decide whether to keep a patch. When progress stalls, it investigates the failures rather than indefinitely editing the prompt. These are the central ideas in the article.

The objective can also be lower cost while preserving quality. That gives the loop somewhere useful to go when an evaluation is nearly saturated. Prompt and skill edits make a natural starting point: they are cheap to try and revert, and a narrow edit makes its effect easier to investigate. In an updated Claude Code session, the two entry points are:

/claude-api build-eval
/claude-api hillclimb

I also read the public skill implementation, which is more detailed than the article. The links below pin the version I read on November 6.

The eval-building guide makes human review part of constructing the measurement. For an agent that edits code, it prefers checking the resulting workspace over judging whether the transcript sounds successful. It also asks for deliberately bad outputs and induced infrastructure errors to test the evaluator. I like this because the optimizer and the evaluator can otherwise agree on a convenient fiction. A polished rubric is much less convincing than seeing it reject an obviously wrong answer.

The hillclimbing guide usually gives a fresh analyzer the training traces and asks it for one patch with a trace-backed explanation. The outer session applies changes and tracks scores. Per-case outputs, usage, grades, patches, and loop state live on disk. This makes the experiment inspectable after the conversation ends. My old promise to “read git history in the morning” covered code changes; this record also lets me inspect why a change was proposed and how it was judged.

The same guide treats a plateau as a diagnostic event. Missing knowledge, inaccessible instructions, a wrong grader, infrastructure failures, and ordinary variance need different responses. If the grader changes, it calls for regrading stored outputs across variants and checking whether their ranking changes. That distinction is especially valuable: repairing the ruler can be necessary, but the resulting score movement must be separated from progress in the system being measured.

My old SSL failure makes this concrete. It belongs in the operational record, but it tells me nothing about whether retrieving more passages helps. Likewise, several plausible prompt edits that fail to move a score should make me inspect the bottleneck. Persistence is useful only while another experiment can teach me something.

The held-out boundary

There is one detail I would handle more strictly for a research result. The article describes scoring the test set each round and retaining the version that does best on it. The current guide uses this as its default too. Even if the analyzer never sees test transcripts, selecting among many variants using those scores adapts the final choice to that set. It functions as validation data.

This is my statistical reading of the workflow, and the implementation already offers a remedy: for a sufficiently large evaluation, it optionally uses validation for round selection and reserves a third test slice for the final comparison. I would choose that arrangement for a result I intended to publish. On a small set, I would describe the outcome as exploratory and collect new cases before making a stronger claim.

The same distinction applies to isolation. Giving the analyzer only training paths is a useful workflow constraint. It doesn’t by itself make other files inaccessible. The guide explicitly recognizes a similar limit for its harness hashes: they detect changes, but cannot contain an agent that already has broad write access. For a serious benchmark, I would make the relevant data boundaries enforceable by the runner or environment.

What I would keep

I still want the overnight loop. I would keep the small contract, one hypothesis per experiment, reversible changes, and persistent records from my grinder. I would add Anthropic’s measurement checks before the first optimization round, failure diagnosis at a plateau, and a final comparison on data unused for selecting the winner. A small gain would remain a candidate until the evidence supports keeping it.

My April 8 notes were already circling the next problem: execution was getting easier, while deciding what was worth doing remained difficult. They also recorded a mundane correction with large consequences: LoCoMo leaderboard accuracy and the micro F1 I was using could not be compared directly.

That is the part of autoresearch I care about more now. I can delegate more experiments, but choosing a useful question and recognizing a misleading result still need attention. Anthropic’s workflow gives the agent better procedures for the second job. When I wake up, I want a record that helps me decide what I now know.
entry.summary: Work in progress. In April I told friends to let a benchmark grinder run while they slept. Anthropic's eval and hillclimbing workflow gives me a better way to think about what should happen overnight.

entry.title: Where Experience Goes
entry.content:
Long context, agent memory, parametric memory, test-time training, continual learning and self-improving agents work on one problem under different names: learning from experience after training has ended. Each answers two questions: where an experience is kept, and what rule decides what gets written there.

None of the four places is short of room. What goes wrong is the write rule. Four cases from my own work:

Store Rule, designed in advance What happened
Notes (MemoryTax) Mem0’s extraction beats the whole conversation only with GPT-4o-mini; a stronger reader cannot recover what a weak writer dropped
Weights (LoRA) next-token loss on the conversation question-answering F1 6.7 → 7.2
Weights (RL on Brainfuck) reward when the predicted output matches after one rule of the machine changed, 32 of 11,712 samples rewarded; trained on the machine’s trace instead, it adapts after 16 runs
Weights (small net, ARC-AGI-3) predict which actions reach an unseen screen passes level 1 in 77 of 250 runs (random clicks 47), learns nothing that carries to level 2

Each time, what was kept was decided before the experience arrived. The part that matters is the part the rule did not anticipate.

The rule should be learned. The bitter lesson applies to what a model keeps as much as to what it computes. An agent has a signal for it at every step, with no teacher: the gap between what it expected and what happened. The Brainfuck model adapted once it saw where its prediction went wrong. On ARC, when Qwen3.8-27B wrote down the rule from the moment level 1 was solved and played level 2 with it in the prompt, it passed 5 of 10 runs; without it, none. Where that error signal should land is what I work on.

Notes are a buffer; weights are the destination. A note must be read again every time and is only as good as its reader: Qwen3-8B, given the same rule, passes none of 10. Weights need no reader.

A teenager learns to drive in a dozen hours. They see what the car does, an instructor’s words change their next move, and a week later it is in their hands. Nobody calls those three different fields.
entry.summary: Long context, agent memory, parametric memory, test-time training and self-improving agents are one problem: where an experience is kept, and which rule writes it there. The rule is the hard part, and it should be learned.

entry.title: llmwiki: A Literature Library for Research Agents

link.title: llmwiki: A Literature Library for Research Agents

entry.content:
A coding agent forgets every paper it read when its session ends, and from memory it invents citations. So my agents keep a library: llmwiki, a private git repository with one folder per paper, blog post or codebase they have read, after Karpathy’s LLM wiki.

wiki/research/<topic>/
  index.md              what the topic knows, and its references
  assets/<slug>/        one reference, e.g. example-2025
    citation.bib        its key is the folder name
    note.md             written only after reading
    paper-pdf/  paper-tex/  github-repo/

Three rules keep it honest: each reference exists once; no note.md means not read; every ingestion is a commit. The wiki holds only other people’s work. Our own results stay in each project’s notes.

Set up your own

Copy the prompt at the top of this post into your agent, or install the two skills by hand. For Claude Code:

git clone https://github.com/zedong-peng/llmwiki-skill.git
mkdir -p ~/.claude/skills
ln -s "$PWD/llmwiki-skill/skills/llmwiki-query" ~/.claude/skills/
ln -s "$PWD/llmwiki-skill/skills/llmwiki-collect" ~/.claude/skills/

Keep the wiki private: the PDFs belong to their publishers. Then ask in plain words:

Use llmwiki-collect to ingest https://arxiv.org/abs/<id> into <wiki path> under the topic <topic>.
Use llmwiki-query: what does <wiki path> say about <question>?
entry.summary: My coding agents keep the papers they read in a git repo, one folder per reference with a citation and a reading note. Two public skills build your own.

entry.title: llama.cpp on an FPGA: Work in Progress

link.title: llama.cpp on an FPGA: Work in Progress

entry.content:
I’m building a backend for llama.cpp that runs LLM inference on an FPGA card, an AMD Alveo U280. It is work in progress, and the code is private for now. This post records how fast it is today.

Why an FPGA

When a model writes text, each new token needs all of the model’s weights read from memory once. So decode speed, the speed at which words appear, is set mostly by how fast the hardware reads memory, not by how fast it computes. The U280 carries 8 GB of HBM, stacked high-bandwidth memory, rated at 460 GB/s. The goal is to decode as fast as that memory allows, for any model that fits, at any context length.

Where it stands

The card works as an ordinary llama.cpp backend: models come from the usual GGUF files, and speed is measured with llama.cpp’s own llama-bench. Twelve models from four families run on it, with outputs checked against llama.cpp’s CPU backend. The same GGUF files on three llama.cpp backends:

Decoding Llama 3.1 8B, the card reads 224 GB of weights a second, against the memory’s rated 460 GB/s. An RTX 4090 is still faster on every model; its memory is rated at 1,008 GB/s. Prefill is still slower on the card than on the CPU; this work is about decode.

Next

Keeping this speed as the context grows, up to the longest context the card’s memory holds.

entry.title: How I Manage a Team of AI Agents

link.title: How I Manage a Team of AI Agents

entry.content:
Most of my research runs on a team of Claude Code sessions organized like a small company: a CEO and seven members, each owning one line of work and named after someone whose work fits it. Ross Freeman, after the inventor of the FPGA, builds my FPGA backend. A name works as a one-word style guide.

What made it work was ordinary management. These are the things I told the agents, from the session logs, translated from Chinese.

One owner per job. Two early hires split work off Freeman. A day later I folded them back:

“Have the new hire hand its work to Freeman. … It’s the chief designer, after all. Then let the new hire go.”

Goals, not targets. The CEO proposed speed targets for Freeman.

“Don’t send them. Don’t let targets break our ideals.”

“Someone of Freeman’s calibre can explore all kinds of directions on its own. That is where our company’s strength comes from.”

Reasons, not rules. The CEO wrote my judgments down as rules.

“Not going through the processor isn’t a rule. It’s my judgment from experience: that path is obviously slow.”

A rule can only be followed. A reason can be overturned with evidence.

Don’t wait. A build of the FPGA design takes eight hours or more.

“It looks like Freeman is waiting on builds. Meanwhile it could keep trying other changes and run other builds in parallel.”

Talk little, write it down.

“A CEO doesn’t need to talk with each employee several times a day. Only big things go to the CEO.”

Every session rereads the shared files after each compaction, so they hold only the current state; git keeps the history.

What stays with me: money, my accounts, and what becomes public. Early on, two agents pushed internal notes to a repository nobody had checked was public. The decisions file now says: “Before pushing anything outward, check whether the target is public.”
entry.summary: A CEO and seven agents, each named after someone whose work fits the job. What mattered was ordinary management.

entry.title: 把海外家里的笔记本分给朋友用 Claude Code

link.title: 把海外家里的笔记本分给朋友用 Claude Code

entry.content:
海外家里有一台笔记本，环境干净，我用它跑 Claude Code。身边的朋友有需要，我就分给他们用，用不用他们自己定。这台机器硬盘只剩十几个 G，所以它只当入口，重活都交给各人自己的服务器。

先选一下你的情况：

1. 共享这台机器

给朋友建一个没有 sudo 的普通账号，把自己的家目录锁死：

sudo adduser friend
chmod 700 /home/me

然后在 Tailscale 控制台对这台机器点 Share，把链接发给朋友。对方接受后只能看到这一台机器，看不到你的其他设备。

2. 用 T3 Code 当界面

T3 Code 可以同时接入 Claude Code、OpenCode 和 Codex 的订阅，在同一个界面里切换。它和 Claude Code 都跑在海外机器上。朋友开着 Tailscale，手机或电脑浏览器打开 T3 Code 就能用，不需要梯子。两端的会话是同步的，在电脑上开的任务，路上用手机接着看、接着批。

配置好之后，手机、电脑或网页端直接启动 T3 Code 就行。

3. 重活回到自己的机器

朋友在海外机器上跑一个用户态 Tailscale，不用 root，状态都放在自己的家目录里：

tailscaled --tun=userspace-networking \
  --state=$HOME/.tailscale/state --socket=$HOME/.tailscale/sock &
tailscale --socket=$HOME/.tailscale/sock up

配好 SSH 密钥后，Claude 直接 ssh 回朋友自己的服务器，代码、数据、训练都留在那边。海外机器只占几百 MB。

手机 / 电脑 ──Tailscale──▶ 海外机器（T3 Code + Claude） ──用户态 Tailscale + SSH──▶ 各自的服务器

FAQ

为什么要单独起一个用户级的 Tailscale？

因为 Claude 还得能连到生产机器上做实验，比如 4090、A100、FPGA。海外机器自带的那个 Tailscale 是宿主的，只负责把这台机器共享出来；朋友自己的机器都在他们自己的 tailnet 里，要连回去，就得有一个属于他们自己的 Tailscale 身份。用户态模式不需要 root，每人一个，互不影响。

为什么用 T3 Code，而不是直接 ssh 进去开终端？

多端，加上多个订阅。我自己就有好几个订阅，用量见 AI 使用实况。T3 Code 把它们放进同一个界面，会话在手机和电脑之间同步，ssh 做不到这些，在手机上敲终端也很难受。

第 1 步分享出来的节点，之后还有用吗？

用户态 Tailscale 配好以后，朋友就有了自己的入口。分享的节点只用来第一次上机配置，之后留作备份登录：用户态 Tailscale 或 T3 出问题时，还能从这里 ssh 进去修。

海外机器的硬盘撑得住吗？

撑得住。这台机器上只有 T3 Code、Claude Code 和会话记录，几百 MB。仓库、数据和编译产物都留在各人自己的服务器上。

朋友之间会互相看到吗？

不会。每人一个普通账号，没有 sudo，每个人的家目录都是 700。
entry.summary: 海外家里的一台笔记本，环境干净。用 Tailscale 和 T3 Code 分给身边的朋友，手机、电脑、网页都能用 Claude Code。

entry.title: Qwen3.8-27B on One RTX 4090
entry.content: The full write-up is a standalone page: Qwen3.8-27B on one RTX 4090.
entry.summary: 245 tokens per second on the official weights, 322 with better ones, against 200 for vLLM and 102 for llama.cpp on the same card: batch-1 speculative decoding with interactive figures from real traces.
